Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system was conceived and developed as a utilitarian teaching tool to help blind students read music without Braille, with focus on functional features (singing note names, chords, usability, multi-track control). It was not adapted from an entertainment game, nor described as co-designed in workshops with diverse or disabled stakeholders; instead, it appears to be primarily utility-driven educational software with some engaging aspects, fitting 'mostly utility first'.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: Participants interact with a specific piece of educational software and must complete clearly defined tasks with precise operations (moving within the song, adjusting volumes, muting tracks, changing speed) using the provided interface/keyboard commands. This is a structured, tool-based activity with fixed functionality and clear correct/incorrect ways to perform tasks, aligning best with a game/system with rigid rules rather than open or loosely structured play.

        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The study is a usability test of educational software where participants perform specific interface and music-related tasks (moving within songs, adjusting volumes, muting tracks, etc.). Outcomes depend entirely on users’ ability to operate the software and understand the musical content; there is no randomization or probabilistic element affecting performance. This makes the design entirely skill-based.

        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),

        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),

reasoning: The study is a usability test of single users interacting with educational software; there is no notion of turns, steps, or phases between multiple players, so the closest fit in the given game-oriented scale is that actions are effectively simultaneous rather than turn-based.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The software is a standalone multi-track audio player for practicing music; users load prepared tracks, control playback (mute, loop, speed) and listen while playing their instrument. There is no indication of real-time multi-user interaction or time-critical coordination with others; interaction is between a single user and prerecorded material, which fits an entirely asynchronous design.

        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The software is a teaching/learning tool for individual blind students, with tasks about using the interface and playing along with sung note names. There is no mention of players, opponents, or any competitive mechanics; all activities are oriented toward helping the learner, so the design is entirely collaborative/supportive rather than competitive.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study is a usability test of a single-player educational software tool, not a multiplayer or adversarial game. There are no roles, turns, or player interactions that could be symmetric or asymmetric; the only relevant interpretation is that all participants interact with the system in their own distinct way (blind vs non-blind, keyboard vs GUI), which is closer to entirely asymmetrical than to any notion of symmetry used in the examples. Given the forced-choice requirement, 5 (entirely asymmetrical) is the least-wrong fit.
